(CNN)  -- The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill student body president who was killed this year was shot several times, including in her head, according to her autopsy report released Monday. Unsealed warrants show Eve Carson was abducted and then shot by both men. Eve Carson, 22, was found slain on March 5. Carson's autopsy report lists six gunshot wounds, but says two were probably from the same bullet, according to North Carolina's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. Carson's death shocked the community and drew national attention. An estimated 10,000 people turned out for a service remembering her. Her autopsy -- released after a North Carolina newspaper filed a court motion to have it unsealed -- describes wounds to various parts of Carson's body. It says shotgun wounds to her head and hand "most likely represent a single shot with the hand acting as an intermediate target." One of the other four wounds was also a gunshot to her head. A separate, handwritten summary of the medical examiner's report says Carson was "shot multiple times" and found lying on her back, with one arm bent behind her head. The autopsy says sexual assault testing was done. It does not say whether any sign of sexual assault was found. Two suspects, Demario James Atwater, 22, and Lawrence Alvin Lovette, 17, have been charged with first-degree murder. Lovette's attorney said the warrants against the suspects rely on hearsay. Atwater's attorney cautioned against "any rush to judgment." Court documents released Friday say Carson was kidnapped from her apartment and forced to provide her abductors with ATM access to her bank account before she was shot to death in the early hours of March 5. The documents -- applications for search warrants -- say a confidential informant told police in the days after the death that Atwater had told her he and Lovette had entered Carson's home through an open door and forced Carson to accompany them in her car. The informant said she had talked with Atwater after a picture was displayed on television showing someone attempting to use Carson's ATM card at a convenience store two days after Carson's body was found. The informant said the two men drove Carson to an ATM, obtaining her PIN number from her. "The CW [informant] learned that Carson was forced into the back seat with Atwater, and Lovette drove Carson's vehicle," the court documents said. "That information is consistent with video footage taken from an ATM camera on that date." The witness told police Atwater said the two got about $1,400 from Carson's account. Bank records show that was approximately the amount taken from the account over a two-day period, the documents said. And the informant said that both suspects shot Carson, according to one of the affidavits. "This information was corroborated by crime scene search information that two separate weapons were used in the homicide," the documents said. The documents said police believe Carson was subjected to a sexual assault "of an unknown nature" and asked for a search warrant to collect DNA swabs from the suspects. But Orange County, North Carolina, District Attorney Jim Woodall told CNN Friday the collection and testing done on Carson's body was routine, and authorities do not believe she was sexually assaulted. Prosecutors had fought to keep her autopsy sealed. Following a motion by the Raleigh News & Observer newspaper, prosecutors agreed to allow the report's release. Carson, a native of Athens, Georgia, was a pre-medicine student double-majoring in political science and biology. She was a recipient of the university's prestigious Morehead Scholarship and a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honor society, UNC has said.

Carson, a senior and Morehead-Cain Scholar from Athens, Georgia, was found dead early on **March 5, 2008**, on a residential street near the UNC campus. Her killing shocked Chapel Hill and the university community, where she was widely known for her campus leadership and public service.

Autopsy findings released by the North Carolina medical examiner showed that Carson died from **multiple gunshot wounds**. Authorities said she had been shot several times with a handgun and also suffered a fatal shotgun wound.

According to reports on the autopsy, Carson sustained gunshot injuries to multiple parts of her body, and the medical examiner concluded that the shotgun wound to the head was fatal. The findings supported investigators’ theory that Carson was killed after being abducted and robbed.

The medical evidence indicated the attack was violent and involved more than one weapon. Investigators later said ballistic evidence and other forensic findings helped connect suspects to the crime.

## Allegations in Unsealed Warrants

Search warrants and related court documents that were unsealed during the investigation laid out the prosecution’s theory of the case: Carson was allegedly abducted from near her home, forced into her own vehicle, taken to automated teller machines, and robbed before being killed.

According to the warrants, investigators believed Carson’s **Toyota Highlander** was used during the crime. The documents alleged that her bank card was used in the hours before her body was discovered, including attempts to withdraw money from ATMs. Surveillance images from bank machines became a key part of the investigation and were publicly circulated as police sought to identify suspects.

The warrants also alleged that Carson was forced to provide access to her bank account, and that the suspects drove her around Chapel Hill and Durham before taking her to the area where she was shot. Investigators said financial records, surveillance footage, witness information and forensic evidence helped build the case.

Court documents further alleged links between the suspects and items connected to Carson, including her vehicle and financial cards. The unsealed materials portrayed the killing as part of a robbery and kidnapping that escalated into murder.

## Charges Against Demario Atwater and Lawrence Lovette

Two men were ultimately charged in Carson’s killing:

- **Demario James Atwater**, who was 21 at the time  
- **Lawrence Alvin Lovette Jr.**, who was 17 at the time  

Both were charged in state court with offenses including:

- **First-degree murder**
- **First-degree kidnapping**
- **Armed robbery**
- **Felony larceny**
- **Possession of stolen property**

Lovette was later convicted in state court of first-degree murder and related charges in Carson’s death. Because he was a juvenile at the time of the crime, later sentencing issues were affected by evolving U.S. Supreme Court rulings on mandatory life-without-parole sentences for juveniles.

## A Case That Shook Chapel Hill

Carson’s death devastated UNC-Chapel Hill, where she was remembered as an exceptionally engaged student leader with a deep commitment to service. Thousands attended memorial events after her killing, and the case prompted widespread discussion about campus safety, violent crime and juvenile sentencing.

Prosecutors argued that Carson was a random victim targeted for robbery, while investigators described the crime as a kidnapping that ended in an execution-style killing. The autopsy findings, ATM evidence, surveillance images and allegations in the unsealed warrants became central to the cases against Atwater and Lovette.

A Morehead-Cain Scholar, Carson studied biology and political science and was involved in a wide range of academic and service work. She participated in student government, campus committees and community programs, and she pursued interests in health, poverty, education and international development. Friends and professors described her as a student who moved easily between intellectual rigor and personal kindness, with a talent for making others feel heard.

After her death, thousands gathered on the UNC campus for vigils and memorial events. University leaders described her as one of the school’s most extraordinary students, and scholarships and service initiatives were later created in her memory.

The criminal cases against the two men accused in her death proceeded separately. Atwater later pleaded guilty in federal court to charges related to kidnapping, carjacking and firearms offenses and received a life sentence. He also faced state charges. Lovette, who was a teenager at the time of the killing, was prosecuted in state court and convicted in Carson’s death.

For many in Chapel Hill, the release of the autopsy report reopens a painful chapter. But media attorneys and open-records advocates said the document is an important part of the public account of a crime that led to major court proceedings, extensive police work and lasting changes in how the community remembered one of its most prominent student leaders.

Carson’s family and friends have long emphasized that her life should not be defined by the violence of her death. In public statements after the killing, those who knew her urged people to remember her compassion, ambition and belief in service.

“She had a way of seeing what was possible,” one university official said in the aftermath of her death. “That is what people here continue to carry with them.”
